open.title: Two people watch the same sky turn opposite ways
open.mini: From Europe the stars turn counter-clockwise about a point in the north. From the southern hemisphere they turn clockwise about a point in the south. A sign, not a degree.
open.text: Point a camera at the sky for an hour and the stars draw arcs. From Europe they turn counter-clockwise about a point in the north; from the southern hemisphere they turn clockwise about a point in the south. The place shown is named above the text, with the positions of its fixed point in each model. On the globe, facing south, the sky turns clockwise about a fixed point due south, at an altitude equal to the latitude [2]. On the flat disc, the same observer would have to face north and see the sky turn counter-clockwise. The stars are real, from the Hipparcos catalogue [1]. The difference is a sign, and a sign is the hardest thing for a model to get wrong quietly.
open.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: star trails from the southern hemisphere turning counter-clockwise about a point in the north.
axis.title: Why a spinning dome cannot reverse the sky
axis.mini: The sky's sense of rotation is the sign of ω·û: the spin axis against the direction you look. On a disc, ω points up for everyone, so everyone sees the same sense. No dome height changes that.
axis.text: For any rigid rotation, the sense you see, clockwise or counter-clockwise, is the sign of ω·û, where ω is the rotation axis and û the direction you look. Reversing it means crossing the plane where ω·û = 0; nothing else does it, not distance, size or speed. On a globe, observers north and south look at opposite ends of the axis, so they see opposite senses. On a flat disc, everyone shares the same up; the dome turns about a vertical, so ω points up for everyone and the fixed point sits above every horizon. The flat model does not get the reversal wrong: it cannot produce it at all, whatever height it gives the stars. The arrow lengths carry no units.
axis.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: the same sense of rotation seen from every place on Earth.
dome.title: The flat model's sky: a dome over a disc
dome.mini: On a flat disc, the stars turn on a dome at height h above the centre. From a distance r, the fixed point stands at atan(h/r) above the horizon: always above it, for everyone.
dome.text: The flat model's sky, seen edge-on and from above. The stars turn on a dome at height h above the centre of the disc, each at a distance ρ from the axis, and the hour angle θ carries them round. An observer at a distance r from the centre sees the fixed point at an altitude of atan(h/r), always above the horizon and always in the direction of the centre, that is, north. That is the model's one free parameter, h, and every star test on this subject has to let it take any value. The dome is drawn far lower than any flat model claims.
dome.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: one dome height h that puts the fixed point at the altitude observed from every place.
sphere.title: Pole, zenith and star: the altitude formula
sphere.mini: On the sphere of directions, the pole, your zenith and a star make a triangle. Its sides give any star's altitude from your latitude, its declination and the time, and put the pole at an altitude equal to your latitude.
sphere.text: On a globe, a star's altitude comes from one spherical triangle on the sphere of directions: the celestial pole, your zenith and the star. The pole is 90° − φ from the zenith, the star 90° − δ from the pole, and the angle between them at the pole is the hour angle. From that triangle, the pole stands at an altitude equal to your latitude φ, the rule every navigator uses [1], and every star's altitude through the night follows with no free parameter. This is a sphere of directions, not of distances: the stars' distances do not enter.
sphere.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: star altitudes that depart from this formula as one travels, in the way a dome of finite height predicts.
sky.title: The shape of a star trail
sky.mini: On a globe every star trail is a circle about the fixed point, from anywhere. On a flat disc, only an observer at the centre sees circles; everyone else sees slanted ovals whose radius varies by a factor of two.
sky.text: A star trail is a circle on the sky if and only if the observer stands on the axis of the circle the star describes. On a globe every observer does, since the axis runs through the Earth's centre and the stars are far away: all trails are circles about the fixed point, from any place. On the flat disc, the stars circle an axis over the centre of the map, so only an observer at the centre sees circles. Everyone else sees an oblique cone over a circle, and the trail's angular radius from the fixed point varies by a factor of two around one turn. The place, date and view are named above the text; the stars are real [1].
sky.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: star trails photographed away from the North Pole that are lopsided about the fixed point, as the disc predicts.
meridian.title: The meridian: each star crosses at φ ± p
meridian.mini: On the meridian, the pole stands at your latitude φ. A star at a distance p from the pole culminates at φ + p and at φ − p twelve hours later. Two altitudes, one rule, anywhere.
meridian.text: Draw the meridian, the north-south line through your zenith. On a globe the pole stands on it at an altitude equal to your latitude φ. A star at an angular distance p from the pole crosses the meridian twice a day: at φ + p above the pole, and at φ − p below it twelve hours later. If φ − p is negative, the star sets. So the altitudes at which every star culminates follow from one number, your latitude, with no free parameter. On a disc with a dome, the same two altitudes depend on the dome's height and your distance from the centre, and change differently from place to place. The drawing is schematic.
meridian.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: culmination altitudes that do not follow φ ± p as one travels north or south.
proj.title: Lenses do not make or unmake a circle
proj.mini: Star trails photograph as ovals, on either model, because of the lens. But a lens is a radial map: it cannot make a symmetric trail lopsided or the reverse. Against the image of a perfect circle, the globe's trail fits; the disc's does not.
proj.text: Star trails photograph as ovals, whichever shape the Earth has, because lenses map the sky onto a flat sensor. The focal length deforms nothing: it only scales the image. The projection law and residual distortion do change shapes, but every one of them is a radial map: it moves each point along the line to the centre of the image and never changes its angle about the centre. So no lens can make a trail that is symmetric about the fixed point lopsided, or the reverse. The dashed curve is the image of a perfect circle about the fixed point through the same lens and framing. On a globe the trail lies on it; on the disc it hugs it on one side and falls away on the other. The lens and place are named above the text.
proj.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: trails that sit off the image of a perfect circle on one side, in the direction the disc predicts.
rhythm.title: Equal times, equal angles
rhythm.mini: Cut a star trail into equal time intervals. On a globe each piece sweeps the same angle about the fixed point, 15.041° per hour, for any star, anywhere. On a disc the pieces stretch and bunch.
rhythm.text: Cut a long exposure into equal intervals, with an intervalometer or a card held over the lens, and the trail becomes a row of dashes. On a globe each dash sweeps exactly the same angle about the fixed point: 15.041° per hour [1], for any star, at any latitude, with no free parameter. On the flat disc the star moves toward the observer and away again during the night, so the dashes stretch and bunch around the fixed point. The test needs one camera, one night and a protractor. The drawing is schematic.
rhythm.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: equal time intervals sweeping unequal angles about the fixed point.
rate.title: One place, one night, one photograph
rate.mini: A star trail cut into equal time steps, seen from the place named above. On a globe every step sweeps 15.041° about the fixed point. A protractor on a print decides it, whatever the lens.
rate.text: The one star test that needs neither travel nor anyone else's data. Photograph a trail in equal time steps from the place named above the text. On a globe every step sweeps the same angle about the fixed point, 15.041° per hour [1]; on the disc the steps stretch and bunch. The test is immune to the lens: aimed at the fixed point, that point becomes the centre of the image, and any radial distortion preserves angles about the centre exactly. Measure with a protractor on a print. It is strong at middle and southern latitudes, weak near the pole where the trail radius collapses, and impossible at the equator, where no trail closes. The stars are real [2].
rate.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: unequal angles between equal time steps, stretching and bunching as the disc predicts.
season.title: Always up, seasonal, or never seen
season.mini: On a globe, your latitude sorts every constellation into three classes: always up, seasonal, or never seen. On a flat disc under a dome, every star is always above every horizon.
season.text: On a globe a constellation falls into one of three classes, decided by its declination compared with 90° minus your latitude: it never sets, it rises and sets with the seasons, or it never rises at all. Near Paris, the Southern Cross is never seen; from Melbourne it never sets. On the flat disc there is one class only: a star's altitude is atan(h/d), positive everywhere and always, so everything would always be up, everywhere. Seasonality by itself proves nothing, since a dome turning at the sidereal rate reproduces it; the test is which constellations never set and which never rise, and from where. The place is named above the text; every line can be checked against the U.S. Naval Observatory's service [2]. The stars are real [1].
season.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: every constellation visible, at some hour, from every latitude.
radec.title: The sky has a map: right ascension and declination
radec.mini: The stars keep their places among themselves, so their directions are mapped on a sphere. Declination is the latitude of that map, right ascension its longitude, counted in hours from the March equinox. Sirius: 6 h 45 min, −16.7°.
radec.text: The angle between two stars is the same tonight and next month, from Europe and from Australia. Their directions can therefore be drawn once on a sphere around the observer, and each star gets two numbers. Declination is the latitude of that map: 0° on the celestial equator, +90° and −90° at the two poles the sky turns about. Right ascension is its longitude, counted eastwards from the point where the Sun crosses the equator in March, in hours because the sky turns once in 24 sidereal hours. Both are measured with a telescope on the meridian and a clock: an altitude and a time. The sphere shown carries the 960 brightest stars of the Hipparcos catalogue [1]. It is a map of directions only; the distances of the stars are not on it.
radec.verdict: Would favour neither model: the two angles only say where a star is on the sky. They are what every other test of the star trails is written in.
prec.title: The stars stay, the grid moves: precession
prec.mini: The axis the sky turns about swings round a circle 23.4° wide in 25,772 years, 50.3″ a year. The pole star changes: Thuban about 2800 BC, Polaris now, Vega about AD 13,700. Every star's coordinates slide, which is why catalogues are dated.
prec.text: From one night to the next a star's right ascension and declination do not change by anything an eye can see. Over centuries they do, because the grid itself moves: the celestial pole travels round the pole of the ecliptic at 50.3″ a year [2], one turn in about 25,772 years if the rate stayed as it is. Hipparchus found it about 129 BC from the position of Spica [3]. Polaris was 12° from the pole in his time and is 0.6° from it today; Thuban was the pole star about 2800 BC and Vega will be near the pole about AD 13,700. The stars drawn are those of Hipparcos [1]; the rate and the tilt are held at their present values, so far dates are good to a century or two.
prec.verdict: Would favour neither model: a dome can be given a swinging axis as easily as a globe. Precession is shown because star coordinates cannot be read without their date.
pm.title: Each star also drifts on its own
pm.mini: Stars are not quite fixed: each has its own proper motion. Barnard's star crosses the Moon's width in 174 years, Sirius in 1,340. In 100,000 years the Big Dipper loses its shape: five of its stars travel together, Dubhe and Alkaid do not.
pm.text: Besides the sliding of the whole grid, every star moves a little across the sky on its own. Halley found it in 1718: Sirius and Arcturus stood more than half a degree south of where Ptolemy's catalogue had put them [2]. The Hipparcos satellite measured these motions for every bright star [1]: 10.4″ a year for Barnard's star, the fastest known, 3.7″ for α Centauri, 1.3″ for Sirius, 0.05″ for Polaris. Carried along straight lines for 100,000 years, they undo the Big Dipper: five of its seven stars travel together and keep their figure, Dubhe and Alkaid go another way. The motion towards or away from us is left out, so the angles are right and the brightnesses are not shown.
pm.verdict: Would favour neither model: proper motions are angles measured on the sky. They show how slowly the map of the stars goes out of date: a naked eye needs centuries to notice.
vis.title: Southern stars from the north, northern stars from the south
vis.mini: On a globe, latitude φ hides only the cap of sky within φ of the far pole. Paris sees 83 % of the celestial sphere, Sirius included; Canopus never rises there and stands 7° high in Cairo. Under a flat dome, every star would be up everywhere.
vis.text: A star is called southern or northern by the sign of its declination, not by where one must stand to see it. On a globe the horizon of latitude φ hides only the cap of sky within φ of the far pole, and a star culminates at 90° − |φ − δ|. Paris therefore sees every star north of declination −41°, 83 % of the sphere: Sirius, a southern star, is the brightest of its winter nights. Melbourne sees Arcturus 33° high and Vega 13° high, and never Polaris. Canopus never rises in Paris and culminates 7° above Cairo; Aristotle already noted that stars are seen in Egypt and Cyprus that are not seen further north [2]. Star positions: Hipparcos, moved to 2026 [1]. Under a flat dome every star stays above the horizon of every place.
vis.verdict: Would favour the flat plane: Canopus or the Southern Cross seen from Paris, or Polaris seen from Melbourne, on any night.
